22	\begin{abstract}
23	% Beat 1: Context
24	AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
25	tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
26	to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
27	pipelines need aggregate views---not just per-execution debugging.
28

31	hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
32	across sessions by semantic work category. CPU flame graphs solve the
33	equivalent aggregation problem for programs, but they rely on
34	deterministic function names; agent prompts are natural language and
35	cannot be folded directly.
36	
37	% Beat 3: This paper

39	recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition. An
40	\emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity; an
41	\emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
42	Sessions and spans become optional fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
43	\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
44	backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
45	produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
46	both developers and analysis agents.
47

51	(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work

53	fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure
54	above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets.
55	\end{abstract}

59	%% ===================================================================
60	\section{Introduction}
61	
62	AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
63	calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
64	labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
65	thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
66	to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
67	tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
68	distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
69	tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
70	Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
71	events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
72	single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
73	that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
74	distribution grouped by semantic work category.
75	
76	CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame
77	graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples into
78	a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
79	\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
80	Agent traces break this assumption---prompts are natural language, and
81	two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters. We develop
82	this gap and the design requirements it implies in
83	\S\ref{sec:background}.
84	
85	The central insight is that agent observability requires
86	\emph{profiling}---aggregate, cross-session cost attribution grouped by
87	user intent (which we call \emph{semantic} to distinguish from
88	execution-structural groupings like sessions or spans)---not only
89	per-execution debugging, and that the obstacle to
90	applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of
91	natural-language identifiers. This paper presents \toolname, a profiler
92	that restores aggregate flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The
93	profiler is built on two abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform
94	weighted record for any agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack}
95	(a field projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace
96	identifiers are operation fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
97	\emph{Intent recognition}---mapping free-form prompts to stable labels
98	through pluggable backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, or
99	unsupervised clustering)---restores the deterministic-label precondition
100	that flame-graph folding requires.
101	
102	Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping: Datadog LLM
103	Observability clusters user messages by topic, and Laminar extracts
104	structured signals from traces. These characterize \emph{input
105	distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions'') but not
106	\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
107	token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
108	aggregation where width represents cost.
109	
110	This paper makes three contributions:
111	
112	\begin{enumerate}
113	\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
114	  We show that the aggregation gap in agent observability---fixed
115	  session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic category---is closed
116	  by combining uniform operation records with query-time stack
117	  projections, once intent recognition restores deterministic labels
118	  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
119	\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
120	  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
121	  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
122	  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
123	  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
124	\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
125	  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
126	  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
127	  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
128	  summaries (RQ2), and that mapping-derived labels agree with
129	  ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
130	  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
131	\end{enumerate}

134	\section{Background and Motivation}
135	\label{sec:background}
136	
137	\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}
138	
139	Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
140	hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
141	containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
142	key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
143	\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
144	Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
145	tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.
146	
147	These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
148	skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
149	nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
150	This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
151	span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
152	the execution context.
153	
154	\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}
155	
156	Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
157	events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
158	aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
159	ways.
160	
161	\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
162	A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
163	may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases; splitting by
164	session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
165	performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
166	merged without external logic.
167	
168	\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
169	Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
170	\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
171	\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
172	LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.
173	
174	\paragraph{Concrete example.}
175	In a real development project, the system effect
176	\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
177	across 325 sessions. A flat process summary shows a single counter; no
178	existing trace tool can disaggregate these executions by the semantic
179	intent that triggered them. We quantify this disaggregation in
180	RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).
181	
182	\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}
183	
184	CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
185	A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
186	weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
187	ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge; width
188	represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
189	\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
190	frames.
191	
192	Agent traces break this precondition. As noted in \S1, prompts are
193	natural language and lack deterministic identifiers; tool calls, GUI
194	actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
195	families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.
196	
197	These observations yield three design requirements:
198	
199	\begin{description}
200	\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
201	  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
202	  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
203	  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
204	  objects.
205	\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
206	  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
207	  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
208	  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
209	\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
210	  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
211	  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
212	  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
213	\end{description}
214	
215	%% ===================================================================
216	\section{Design}
217	\label{sec:design}
218	
219	The three requirements from \S\ref{sec:background} drive the design.
220	We introduce two abstractions---operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
221	operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks})---that satisfy R1 and R2, and a
222	pluggable intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that
223	satisfies R3.
224	
225	\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
226	\label{sec:ops}
227	
228	A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
229	process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
230	abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
231	additive measures.
232	
233	Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
234	\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
235	\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
236	measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
237	call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
238	are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
239	This satisfies R1: the profiler does not need to distinguish event types
240	at the object-model level.
241	
242	\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
243	\label{sec:stacks}
244	
245	An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
246	operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
247	representation:
248	
249	\begin{small}
250	\begin{verbatim}
251	CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
252	Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
253	\end{verbatim}
254	\end{small}
255	
256	\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
257	execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
258	operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
259	semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
260	Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.
261	
262	This directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem from
263	\S\ref{sec:background}: sessions and spans are optional operation fields,
264	not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
265	produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree); excluding
266	it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
267	provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.
268	
269	\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler: it reads recorded traces,
270	not live events. Runtime capture overhead belongs to AgentSight, the
271	live-capture component (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
272	
273	A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
274	selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
275	operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
276	nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
277	views; four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
278	questions:
279	
280	\begin{table}[t]
281	\centering\small
282	\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
283	but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
284	\label{tab:views}
285	\begin{tabular}{llll}
286	\toprule
287	View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
288	\midrule
289	\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
290	\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
291	\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
292	\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
293	\bottomrule
294	\end{tabular}
295	\end{table}

311	\label{fig:architecture}
312	\end{figure}
313	
314	\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
315	\label{sec:intent}
316	
317	Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
318	folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
319	that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
320	this through \emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts to
321	short, stable labels before stack construction.
322	
323	The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:
324	
325	\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
326	The production default. Rules have the form
327	\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
328	\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
329	and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
330	match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
331	observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
332	iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
333	rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
334	version-controllable.
335	
336	\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
337	For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
338	(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
339	per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
340	Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
341	
342	\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
343	TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
344	without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.
345	
346	The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
347	short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
348	and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.
349	
350	\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}
351	
352	For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
353	already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
354	quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
355	\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
356	before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
357	analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
358	fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.
359	
360	This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
361	(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
362	mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
363	stack query works identically on both.
364	
365	%% ===================================================================
366	\section{Implementation}
367	\label{sec:impl}
368	
369	\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).
370	
371	\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
372	The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
373	history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
374	their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
375	calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
376	semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
377	semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
378	instrumentation.
379	
380	\paragraph{Dataset import.}
381	Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
382	(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
383	Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
384	non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.
385	
386	\paragraph{Output formats.}
387	\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
388	\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
389	text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
390	SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
391	the same input and profile spec.
392	
393	\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
394	\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
395	observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
396	capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
397	\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
398	tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
399	run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
400	runs'' (profiling).
401

403	\section{Evaluation}
404	\label{sec:eval}
405	
406	We organize the evaluation around three research questions, followed by
407	case studies and a reproducibility check.
408	
409	\paragraph{Evaluation setup.}
410	We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
411	local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
412	multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
413	observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
414	mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
415	(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through
416	mapping rules. All public traces are real agent or human executions

418	oracle-rich families (AgentRewardBench, SATraj-OS, AgentNet,
419	OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2. No source

422	changing only the stack fields.

447	\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}
448	
449	The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
450	tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
451	directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
452	\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
453	multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.
454	
455	\begin{table}[t]
456	\centering\small
457	\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
458	from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
459	\label{tab:mixing}
460	\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
461	\toprule
462	Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
463	\midrule
464	No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
465	Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
466	Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
467	Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
468	\bottomrule
469	\end{tabular}
470	\end{table}
471	
472	Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
473	sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
474	into mixed buckets: a flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
475	executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
476	\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
477	prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
478	residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
479	sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.
480	
481	A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
482	appears under 48 distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor})
483	accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
484	\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
485	others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.
486	
487	As a robustness check, a label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within
488	each session) confirms the separation is not random ($p = 0.001$). The
489	primary evidence is the mixing reduction itself; the permutation test
490	verifies statistical significance. RQ3 evaluates label quality from a
491	complementary angle: agreement with ground-truth annotations on public
492	datasets.
493	
494	RQ1 also tests whether query-time stack selection (R2) adds value
495	beyond flat label grouping. The same two-abstraction model covers all 15
496	public trace families (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) without type-specific
497	objects. On the four oracle-rich families, the same 13{,}265 operations
498	fold from 9~dataset stacks to 57~phase stacks, 226~semantic stacks,
499	455~action stacks, or 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by changing only the
500	stack fields. This is not achievable with a flat GROUP BY on a single
501	label: different stack depths answer different questions (task-level
502	budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
503	the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.
504	
505	The multi-view design is further validated by metric divergence. The
506	\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
507	only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
508	\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
509	tokens.
510	
511	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
512	\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}
513	
514	A profiler is useful if its top groups correspond to real problems: the
515	categories that concentrate failures, safety violations, or wasted
516	effort should appear at the top of the ranked output. RQ2 tests this
517	correspondence. The methodology is analogous to injecting known
518	bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation: public benchmark datasets
519	provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
520	human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
521	resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden
522	positives.
523	
524	\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
525	Six tasks across four datasets: AgentRewardBench looping and
526	side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant
527	step, and OSWorld-Human group start. Together: 34{,}539 operations,
528	3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
529	raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
530	visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).
531	
532	\paragraph{Localization results.}
533	
534	\begin{table*}[t]
535	\centering\small
536	\caption{RQ2 hidden-label localization (medians across six tasks).
537	Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.}
538	\label{tab:localization}
539	\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
540	\toprule
541	Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
542	\midrule
543	flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
544	fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
545	dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\
546	raw-action:query-aware & 0 & 0.274 & 0.244 & 0.220 & 0.151 & 0.333 & 0.037 & --- \\
547	op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\
548	op-stack:oracle-upper & 1 & 0.599 & 0.300 & 0.403 & 0.044 & 0.564 & 0.012 & --- \\
549	label-drilldown:oracle & 1 & 1.000 & 0.670 & 0.797 & 0.115 & 1.000 & 0.038 & --- \\
550	\bottomrule
551	\end{tabular}
552	\end{table*}
553	
554	Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
555	recover all positives but require inspecting everything
556	(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
557	(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
558	2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
559	9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
560	recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.
561	
562	The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. The comparison also
563	serves as evidence for the two-abstraction model (C1): fixed-session
564	drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions that
565	fix the hierarchy at session or dataset boundaries. Operation stacks
566	subsume both as special cases (include \texttt{session} in the stack
567	to recover fixed-session; include \texttt{dataset} to recover
568	dataset-native). On localization, operation stacks improve top-five
569	recall over fixed-session on 5/6 tasks, reduce median group count by
570	45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat summaries.
571	Fixed-session drilldown retains lower work-to-first-positive on 4/6
572	tasks: profilers and debuggers are complementary. Bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation
573	(2{,}000 trials) confirm stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\%
574	prevalence/group-size null on all six tasks.
575	
576	\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}
577	
578	Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
579	rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
580	patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
581	delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
582	emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
583	changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
584	localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
585	(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
586	OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
587	insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
588	fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
589	74, with an explicit work tradeoff.
590	
591	Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
592	(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
593	misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
594	use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.
595	
596	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
597	\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}
598	
599	RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
600	label-derivation pipeline itself. For structured traces (public
601	datasets), we evaluate the \emph{mapping} path against ground-truth
602	annotations. For free-form traces (real sessions), we evaluate the
603	\emph{intent-recognition} path at the scale and syntax level; quality
604	assessment of the LLM/regex tagger against free-form ground truth
605	remains future work.
606	
607	\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
608	On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
609	(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
610	hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local
611	3B-parameter model. Final tag failures: 0. On a fixed set of 300
612	redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce
613	900/900 syntactically valid outputs; p95 latencies are 23, 18, and
614	31\,ms respectively.
615	
616	\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
617	Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
618	ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation:
619	for each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
620	measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
621	the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
622	mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.
623

625	\centering\small
626	\caption{Leave-dataset-out mapping quality. V-measure between
627	mapping-derived \texttt{phase} and native \texttt{action} labels.
628	13{,}265 total operations across 9 held-out evaluations.}
629	\label{tab:vmeasure}
630	\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
631	\toprule
632	Held-out dataset & Ops & V-measure & Boundary F1 \\
633	\midrule
634	mind2web & 774 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\
635	webshop-expert & 2{,}504 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\

646	
647	Table~\ref{tab:vmeasure} shows the results. On 7/9 datasets, V-measure
648	exceeds 0.7, indicating strong agreement between mapping-derived and
649	native labels. The two low-scoring datasets (toolbench, api-bank) have

651	cover. Mapping reduces unique stacks on 6/9 datasets with zero negative
652	regressions.
653	
654	A supervised boundary-derivation backend further validates the field
655	pipeline. On OSWorld-Human held-out adjacent pairs, a learned boundary
656	predictor achieves F1~0.77, beating the best simple baseline
657	(\texttt{always\_boundary}, F1~0.71). Learned backends beat simple
658	baselines on 4/5 tested boundary families, while AgentRewardBench
659	looping is fully explained by \texttt{repeat\_signal\_change} (baseline
660	F1~1.0). This supports field derivation as a guarded configuration
661	step, not automatic intent discovery.
662	
663	\paragraph{Cross-configuration consistency.}
664	Two mapping-rule variants (differing in API/tool phase precedence) run
665	on the same 13{,}265 operations produce identical V-measure on 7/9
666	datasets; the two divergent datasets (api-bank, toolbench) differ by
667	$\leq$0.17 in V-measure. This suggests that mapping quality is robust
668	to minor rule variations on well-covered action vocabularies. Direct
669	cross-backend comparison between the regex and LLM taggers on the same
670	free-form prompts remains future work.
671	
672	\paragraph{Semantic quality versus syntactic validity.}
673	Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
674	achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
675	concentrates on a narrow label set, outputting
676	\texttt{localization}/\texttt{localized} disproportionately. The 3B
677	model produces a broader vocabulary (328 unique prompt tags) but includes
678	noisy entries (\texttt{agentsightsm}, \texttt{testcodex}). A
679	display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
680	through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
681	93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
682	noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
683	ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.
684	
685	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
686	\subsection{Case Studies}
687	
688	RQ1--RQ3 evaluate mechanism and fidelity quantitatively. This subsection
689	demonstrates the aggregate, cross-session insights that motivate the
690	profiling abstraction---the kind of questions that per-event timeline
691	views structurally cannot answer. We profile the same 325-session
692	development project and report four representative observations.
693	
694	\paragraph{Budget distribution.}
695	The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
696	\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
697	\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A
698	timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot produce this
699	distribution without external aggregation. The stack further decomposes
700	each category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
701	\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}.
702	
703	\paragraph{Cross-session duplication.}
704	The \texttt{files} view shows \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across
705	different sessions repeatedly accessing the same source files under
706	\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these into a single
707	wide bar; a timeline shows each as an isolated event.
708	
709	\paragraph{Metric divergence.}
710	The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views share only 7/10 top prompt
711	categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait)
712	but 93rd by tokens; \texttt{benchmark} prompts show the reverse.
713	
714	\paragraph{Path and network auditing.}
715	The \texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt
716	categories (\texttt{anthropic.com}, \texttt{crates.io},
717	\texttt{github.com}). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses
718	outside the project root (\texttt{external/home},
719	\texttt{external/tmp}), supporting security auditing.

736	\subsection{Reproducibility}
737	
738	All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
739	re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations); all produce
740	identical semantic output. Median runtime: 1.6\,s per spec (p95:
741	2.8\,s). Deterministic-output mode stabilizes raw-byte output: 76/76
742	achieve both semantic and raw-byte determinism.
743	
744	%% ===================================================================
745	\section{Related Work}
746	
747	\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
748	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
749	folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
750	hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
751	pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
752	generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
753	events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
754	\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
755	difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
756	semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
757	recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
758	agent-trajectory labels.
759	
760	\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
761	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
762	spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
763	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
764	visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
765	AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
766	covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
767	single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
768	charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
769	cross-session aggregate profiling.
770	Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
771	Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
772	toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
773	distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
774	\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
775	token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
776	aggregation where width represents cost.
777	
778	\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
779	AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
780	constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
781	TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
782	semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
783	miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
784	fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
785	\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
786	categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
787	or generate repeated system effects across sessions.
788	
789	%% ===================================================================
790	\section{Discussion}
791	
792	\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
793	Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
794	(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
795	investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
796	attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
797	case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
798	the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
799	tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
800	understand why.
801	
802	\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
803	The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
804	designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
805	developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
806	scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
807	and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
808	coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
809	and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
810	regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:design}) already uses. This positions
811	semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
812	for human inspection.
813	
814	\paragraph{Limitations.}
815	The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
816	on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
817	containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
818	multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
819	generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
820	not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
821	flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
822	the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
823	contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
824	operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
825	engineering work, not design obstacles.
826	
827	%% ===================================================================
828	\section{Conclusion}
829	
830	Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
831	that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
832	make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
833	abstractions---operations and operation stacks---close this gap once
834	intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
835	confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge,
836	localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
837	fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
838	ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.
839	
840	The main limitation is single-project real-session data; multi-project
841	evaluation and direct cross-backend tagger comparison are next steps.
842	The most impactful direction is trace-ecosystem integration:
843	importing OpenTelemetry and LangSmith traces as operations would let
844	\toolname profile any instrumented agent without a custom parser.

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
% Beat 1: Context
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views---not just per-execution debugging.

% Beat 2: Problem
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. CPU flame graphs solve the
equivalent aggregation problem for programs, but they rely on
deterministic function names; agent prompts are natural language and
cannot be folded directly.

% Beat 3: This paper
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition. An
\emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity; an
\emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
Sessions and spans become optional fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
both developers and analysis agents.

% Beat 4: Results
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
by 90\% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus
fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure
above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
distribution grouped by semantic work category.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame
graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples into
a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this assumption---prompts are natural language, and
two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters. We develop
this gap and the design requirements it implies in
\S\ref{sec:background}.

The central insight is that agent observability requires
\emph{profiling}---aggregate, cross-session cost attribution grouped by
user intent (which we call \emph{semantic} to distinguish from
execution-structural groupings like sessions or spans)---not only
per-execution debugging, and that the obstacle to
applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of
natural-language identifiers. This paper presents \toolname, a profiler
that restores aggregate flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The
profiler is built on two abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform
weighted record for any agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack}
(a field projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace
identifiers are operation fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\emph{Intent recognition}---mapping free-form prompts to stable labels
through pluggable backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, or
unsupervised clustering)---restores the deterministic-label precondition
that flame-graph folding requires.

Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping: Datadog LLM
Observability clusters user messages by topic, and Laminar extracts
structured signals from traces. These characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions'') but not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
  We show that the aggregation gap in agent observability---fixed
  session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic category---is closed
  by combining uniform operation records with query-time stack
  projections, once intent recognition restores deterministic labels
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that mapping-derived labels agree with
  ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}

Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.

These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
the execution context.

\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}

Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
ways.

\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases; splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
merged without external logic.

\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.

\paragraph{Concrete example.}
In a real development project, the system effect
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
across 325 sessions. A flat process summary shows a single counter; no
existing trace tool can disaggregate these executions by the semantic
intent that triggered them. We quantify this disaggregation in
RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).

\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge; width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition. As noted in \S1, prompts are
natural language and lack deterministic identifiers; tool calls, GUI
actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
  objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

The three requirements from \S\ref{sec:background} drive the design.
We introduce two abstractions---operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks})---that satisfy R1 and R2, and a
pluggable intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that
satisfies R3.

\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
\label{sec:ops}

A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
additive measures.

Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
This satisfies R1: the profiler does not need to distinguish event types
at the object-model level.

\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
\label{sec:stacks}

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.

This directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem from
\S\ref{sec:background}: sessions and spans are optional operation fields,
not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree); excluding
it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.

\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler: it reads recorded traces,
not live events. Runtime capture overhead belongs to AgentSight, the
live-capture component (\S\ref{sec:impl}).

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
views; four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
questions:

\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
\label{sec:intent}

Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
this through \emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts to
short, stable labels before stack construction.

The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).

\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
instrumentation.

\paragraph{Dataset import.}
Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.

\paragraph{Output formats.}
\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
the same input and profile spec.

\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
runs'' (profiling).

\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude

primary evidence is the mixing reduction itself; the permutation test
verifies statistical significance. RQ3 evaluates label quality from a
complementary angle: agreement with ground-truth annotations on public
datasets.

RQ1 also tests whether query-time stack selection (R2) adds value
beyond flat label grouping. The same two-abstraction model covers all 15
public trace families (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) without type-specific

budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.

The multi-view design is further validated by metric divergence. The
\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens.

\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

A profiler is useful if its top groups correspond to real problems: the
categories that concentrate failures, safety violations, or wasted
effort should appear at the top of the ranked output. RQ2 tests this
correspondence. The methodology is analogous to injecting known
bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation: public benchmark datasets
provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,

misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but

\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
label-derivation pipeline itself. For structured traces (public
datasets), we evaluate the \emph{mapping} path against ground-truth
annotations. For free-form traces (real sessions), we evaluate the
\emph{intent-recognition} path at the scale and syntax level; quality
assessment of the LLM/regex tagger against free-form ground truth
remains future work.

\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local
3B-parameter model. Final tag failures: 0. On a fixed set of 300
redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce
900/900 syntactically valid outputs; p95 latencies are 23, 18, and
31\,ms respectively.

display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.

\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
cross-session aggregate profiling.
Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
understand why.

\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:design}) already uses. This positions
semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
for human inspection.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
engineering work, not design obstacles.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
abstractions---operations and operation stacks---close this gap once
intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge,
localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.

The main limitation is single-project real-session data; multi-project
evaluation and direct cross-backend tagger comparison are next steps.
The most impactful direction is trace-ecosystem integration:
importing OpenTelemetry and LangSmith traces as operations would let
\toolname profile any instrumented agent without a custom parser.

The abstract says "semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight." RQ1 says "90.4\%." The conclusion (line 835) says "separates information flat views merge" without a number. The contribution list (line 125) says "90\%." These are consistent enough, but 90% vs 90.4% could confuse a careful reader.

Used as a compound modifier: "flame-graph analysis", "flame-graph frames" (hyphenated) — lines 92, 100, 195, 319, 346.
